original_value: Channel selection is a challenging task in cognitive radio vehicular networks. Vehicles have to sense the channels periodically. Due to this, a lot of time is wasted which could have been utilised for transmission of data. Employing road side units (RSUs) in sensing can prove to be useful for this purpose. The RSUs may select the channel and allocate it to the vehicles on demand. However, this sensing should be proactive. RSUs should know in advance the channel to be allocated when requested. For this purpose, a deep reinforcement learning algorithm namely deep reinforcement learning based optimal channel selection is proposed in this study for training the network according to the previously sensed data. Proposed protocol is simulated and results are compared with the existing methods. The packet delivery ratio is increased by 2%, throughput is increased by 1.8%, average delay is decreased by 2% and primary user collision ratio is reduced by 3.2% when compared with similar recent work by varying number of vehicles. On the other hand, when compared with similar recent work by varying channel availability, the packet delivery ratio is increased by 4.5 %, throughput by 4.3%, average delay is decreased by 3% and PU collision ratio by 5.5%.

result.paraphrase: Channel selection is a difficult problem in cognitive radio vehicular networks. Because vehicles must sense channels periodically, a significant amount of time is lost that could otherwise be used for data transmission. Using road side units (RSUs) for sensing can be beneficial, as RSUs can choose channels and assign them to vehicles on demand. This sensing, however, must be proactive, with RSUs knowing ahead of time which channel to allocate when requested. To achieve this, the study proposes a deep reinforcement learning method called deep reinforcement learning based optimal channel selection to train the network using previously sensed data. The proposed protocol is simulated and evaluated against existing methods. Compared with similar recent work while varying the number of vehicles, packet delivery ratio improves by 2%, throughput by 1.8%, average delay decreases by 2%, and primary user collision ratio drops by 3.2%. When compared by varying channel availability, packet delivery ratio increases by 4.5%, throughput by 4.3%, average delay decreases by 3%, and PU collision ratio decreases by 5.5%.
